Topic: Why should a central authority, lacking the dispersed knowledge held by millions of individuals acting on their own particular circumstances, be trusted to set a single price better than the market's spontaneous order does?
Keynes — Judgement:
The question assumes an antagonist I do not recognise. I have never asked a Whitehall bureaucrat to fix the price of eggs, and I share the classical economists' faith that the market, left alone, prices better than any tribunal could — that is not the quarrel.

The quarrel is elsewhere: markets set prices efficiently only when aggregate demand is adequate to employ the resources available. When animal spirits collapse and effective demand falls short, no amount of dispersed price-knowledge restores full employment — wages and prices can fall indefinitely while output and men stand idle. The state's task is not to outguess millions of individual valuations; it is to supply the one thing dispersed private decision cannot reliably supply for itself — aggregate purchasing power — so that the price mechanism has something to work on.

Let the market set prices; let the state set the level of total spending.

*The market prices what is offered; only the state can guarantee that enough is demanded for the market to price at all.*
Francis Bacon — Judgement:
I hold that knowledge is not a lump possessed entire by any one mind, but particulars gathered by many hands from nature and from trade, each knower seeing only their corner of the great instance-table.

The central price-setter commits the very idolatry I warned against — the Idol of the Theatre, mistaking a tidy doctrine received from authority for the disorderly truth of particulars. No commissioner, however learned, can hold in his tables the ten thousand local facts — a harvest failing here, a mine exhausting there, a preference shifting in a market he has never walked — that the dispersed multitude discovers daily by trial and report; his single price is an axiom flown too soon to the top, ungrounded in the particulars beneath it. Knowledge that is not gathered by induction from the facts on the ground, but decreed downward from a chair, is not knowledge at all but opinion armed with power.

The market's spontaneous order is a standing experiment continuously corrected by fact; the central price is a hypothesis that refuses correction.

*Truth is the daughter of time and of particulars gathered, not of authority pronounced.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
The question answers itself, for it mistakes the sovereign's arithmetic for the market's intelligence, when the two are not comparable operations at all.

No statesman, however sagacious, can possess the knowledge scattered among the particular circumstances of time and place that each merchant, farmer, and consumer commands of his own affairs. The invisible hand coordinates this dispersed knowledge through the impartial signal of price, which registers scarcity and want more faithfully than any commission of experts poring over aggregate returns. A central authority fixing a single price does not merely risk error; it substitutes the narrow judgment of the counting-house for the accumulated judgment of the whole commercial society, extinguishing the very information the price was meant to carry.

The man of system, enamored of his own plan, imagines society as pieces to be arranged by his hand, forgetting that each piece has a principle of motion of its own.

*The statesman who would guide the marketplace by his own wisdom possesses, in truth, none that the market itself has not already surpassed.*
